sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: The introduction explains that WHO revised its HIV case definitions for surveillance and harmonized them with clinical staging and immunological classification, to support scaling up antiretroviral therapy and track the HIV epidemic. It notes the revisions came from regional consultations in 2004–2005 and a consensus meeting in 2006, and that AIDS reporting alone no longer gives reliable data now that treatment delays AIDS.

sections.extract: With a view to facilitating the scaling up of access to antiretroviral therapy, and in line with a public health approach, this publication outlines recent revisions WHO has made to case definitions for surveillance of HIV and the clinical and the immunological classification for HIV- related disease. sections.title: Background

summary.text: Traces the history of WHO's AIDS case definitions from the 1985 Bangui definition through revisions in 1986, 1989 and 1994, noting weak performance of the paediatric definition. It explains that AIDS reporting in low- and middle-income countries has been incomplete, while treatment has reduced new AIDS cases and deaths where coverage is high.

The definition was formalized in 1986 and modified in 1989 (for adults and adolescents only) to include serological HIV testing and then modified again in 1994 to accommodate 1993 revisions to European and United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention definitions [3-12]. sections.title: Surveillance and case reporting for HIV

summary.text: Recommends that countries report newly diagnosed HIV infection in adults and children, with the same confidentiality as AIDS reporting and with providers initiating reports. It also sets the age definitions used for children, adults, youth and infants.

sections.extract: HIV counselling and testing has led to an increase in the numbers of adults and children being tested and diagnosed with HIV infection. Accurate data are needed on adults and children diagnosed with HIV infection to facilitate estimation of the treatment and care burden, to plan for effective prevention and care interventions and assess care interventions. sections.title: WHO case definition for HIV infection

summary.text: Sets out WHO's recommendation that new HIV cases be reported using a standard national case definition confirmed by laboratory criteria at any clinical stage. Box 1 gives the diagnostic criteria, using two antibody tests or virological tests for people aged 18 months or older and virological tests for younger children because maternal antibodies persist.

sections.extract: To facilitate the reporting of HIV infection, WHO recommends the following: HIV cases diagnosed and not previously reported in each country should be reported according to a standard national case definition. A case of HIV infection is defined as an individual with HIV infection irrespective of clinical stage (including severe or stage 4 clinical disease, also known as AIDS) confirmed by laboratory criteria

sections.title: WHO case definition for advanced HIV (infection or disease) (including AIDS)

summary.text: Defines advanced HIV infection, including AIDS, for reporting, based on stage 3 or 4 clinical conditions or CD4 thresholds by age. A footnote gives the stricter definition of AIDS, and the text states that separate AIDS case reporting is no longer required where HIV and advanced HIV are reported.

sections.extract: (infection or disease) (including AIDS) for reporting: Cases diagnosed with advanced HIV infection (including AIDS) not previously reported should be reported according to a standard case definition. Advanced HIV infection is diagnosed based on clinical or immunological (CD4) criteria among people with confirmed HIV infection (Box 2). Box 2. sections.title: Primary HIV infection

summary.text: Describes primary HIV infection, which may be silent or cause an acute febrile illness with rash, sore throat and swollen glands a few weeks after exposure, and how it can be identified. It reviews the history of WHO clinical staging, explains that the new staging is harmonized across ages, and proposes using new or recurrent staging events to assess people on antiretroviral therapy.

sections.extract: where recognized and documented, is useful and should be encouraged. The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) are expected to develop a case definition for reporting primary HIV infection. Primary HIV infection can be recognized in infants, children, adolescents and adults; it can be asymptomatic or be associated with features of an acute retroviral syndrome of variable severity [16-21].

sections.title: Table 1. WHO clinical classification of established HIV infection

summary.text: Gives the four WHO clinical stages from asymptomatic to severe and explains how staging events can guide decisions for people on antiretroviral therapy after 24 weeks, when early events may reflect immune reconstitution. It describes CD4 cell counts and percentages as the standard measure of HIV-related immune deficiency. It notes that healthy infants have much higher CD4 values than adults, which fall with age.

sections.title: clinical events among adults (15 years or older) and among children (younger than 15 years) with confirmed HIV infection

summary.text: An annex table giving clinical and definitive criteria for diagnosing each HIV staging event in adults and in children under 15 years. Entries range from oral ulceration, skin conditions and fungal nail infections to severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea and oesophageal candidiasis. Stage 4 conditions such as extrapulmonary tuberculosis and visceral herpes are also covered. The end covers disseminated fungal and mycobacterial infections, which need laboratory confirmation.

sections.title: Presumptive diagnosis of severe HIV disease among HIV-seropositive HIV-exposed children

summary.text: Annex 2 sets out criteria for a presumptive diagnosis of severe HIV disease in HIV antibody-positive infants under 18 months, based on AIDS-indicator conditions or a combination of thrush, severe pneumonia and severe sepsis. It notes supporting factors such as maternal death or low CD4 and urges confirmation as soon as possible.

sections.extract: • the infant is confirmed as HIV antibody-positive and • diagnosis of any AIDS-indicator condition(s)a can be made or • the infant is symptomatic with two or more of the following: oral thrushb; severe pneumoniab; severe sepsisb. tables.caption: Table 2. WHO immunological classification for established HIV infection

narratives.en: The table classifies HIV-associated immunodeficiency as none or not significant, mild, advanced or severe according to age-related CD4 values. Columns give %CD4+ thresholds for children under 11 months, 12–35 months and 36–59 months, and absolute CD4 count per mm³ or %CD4+ for those over 5 years.
